blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: MSE passes through a square root to become RMSE

blocks.text: MSE, the previous topic, closed with a genuine practical drawback: squaring the raw prediction error also squares its units, producing a result like dollars squared that carries no direct, intuitive real-world meaning to anyone reading it. Root Mean Squared Error, RMSE for short, fixes this with one simple, additional final step: take the square root of MSE, undoing the unit-squaring effect while preserving MSE's core, deliberate sensitivity to large errors.

This combination, MSE's outlier-sensitive squared-error penalty paired with a return to the target variable's original, interpretable units, is precisely what has made RMSE the single most commonly reported regression evaluation metric across machine learning competitions, academic research, and industry practice, and understanding exactly why that combination works so well is the focus of this topic.
2. The Formula

blocks.alt: MSE has its square root taken to produce the RMSE value

blocks.text: RMSE builds directly and simply on MSE, already covered in the previous topic. Starting from MSE, the average of squared prediction errors, RMSE is computed by taking the square root of that entire MSE value. Formally, RMSE equals the square root of the average of the actual value minus the predicted value, squared, across every example in the evaluation dataset.

This single square root operation exactly reverses the unit-squaring effect that made raw MSE difficult to interpret directly. If the underlying target is measured in dollars, MSE ends up in dollars squared, but RMSE, its square root, returns to plain dollars, exactly the same original, directly interpretable units MAE was already measured in, covered two topics ago.
3. Combining the Best of MAE and MSE

blocks.alt: MSE penalizes big errors and MAE gives same units, and RMSE combines both

blocks.text: It is worth stating directly why RMSE has become so popular by comparing it side by side against the two metrics already covered in this module. MAE offers directly interpretable, original-unit results, but treats every error linearly, giving it limited sensitivity to occasional large, potentially important errors. MSE offers strong, deliberate sensitivity to large errors through its squaring step, but produces results in squared units that carry no direct, intuitive real-world meaning.

RMSE inherits MSE's squaring-based sensitivity to large errors directly, since it is built from MSE as its very first step, while also inheriting MAE's directly interpretable, original-unit results, since the final square root step restores those original units. This combination genuinely captures a meaningful strength from each of the two previously covered metrics, without carrying over either one's corresponding weakness in full.

blocks.text: 4. Comparing RMSE Directly Against MAE

blocks.alt: RMSE higher than MAE signals that some big errors exist

blocks.text: Because RMSE and MAE are now both measured in the exact same original target units, they can be compared directly against each other for the same model, and that direct comparison itself reveals useful diagnostic information. Mathematically, RMSE is always greater than or equal to MAE for the same set of predictions, a consequence of how squaring inside RMSE weights larger errors more heavily than MAE's linear averaging does.

When RMSE sits close to MAE for a given model, that indicates the individual prediction errors are fairly uniform in size, with no small number of unusually large errors dominating the picture. When RMSE is noticeably larger than MAE, that gap itself is a useful, direct signal that a handful of larger errors are inflating RMSE substantially above what the more typical, everyday error size, reported by MAE, would otherwise suggest, exactly the kind of diagnostic insight worth checking whenever both metrics are available for the same model.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: Reporting both RMSE and MAE together for the same model, rather than just one or the other, gives a genuinely richer picture of error behavior than either metric alone, since the gap between them directly reveals whether the error distribution is fairly uniform or dominated by a few larger mistakes.

blocks.text: 5. The Most Commonly Reported Regression Metric

This exact combination of properties, outlier sensitivity paired with directly interpretable original units, is precisely why RMSE has become, by a wide margin, the most commonly reported regression evaluation metric in practical use, appearing constantly across machine learning competition leaderboards, academic research papers, and industry benchmark reports.

This widespread adoption makes RMSE worth recognizing as something close to a default expectation when reporting or reading about regression model performance, even though MAE and raw MSE each retain their own genuine, specific advantages for particular situations already covered in their respective topics. When in doubt about which metric to report first, or which metric a given benchmark or competition is likely using, RMSE is the reasonable default assumption.
6. RMSE Still Inherits MSE's Outlier Sensitivity

It is important not to mistake RMSE's restored, interpretable units for a fix to MSE's outlier sensitivity itself; that sensitivity, covered in depth in the MSE topic, remains fully intact in RMSE. Taking a square root at the very end of the calculation does not undo the squaring and disproportionate weighting of large errors that already happened earlier in the computation, inside the MSE step RMSE is built directly on top of.

A single extreme outlier prediction still inflates RMSE substantially, in exactly the same underlying way it inflates MSE, since the square root is simply the final step applied after all of that squaring and averaging has already occurred. RMSE genuinely fixes the units problem covered for MSE, but it deliberately does not, and should not, fix MSE's core statistical behavior around outliers, since that outlier sensitivity is precisely the useful, deliberate property RMSE was built to preserve in the first place.
7. Interpreting an RMSE Value

An RMSE of 8000, for a model predicting house prices in dollars, can be read roughly as a typical error size in dollars, similar in spirit to how MAE is read, but it is worth being precise about an important subtlety: RMSE is not exactly the same quantity as the average absolute error MAE reports, since large errors are weighted more heavily inside RMSE's square root than they would be under MAE's simple linear averaging.

This means RMSE tends to run somewhat higher than MAE for the same set of predictions whenever any meaningfully large errors are present, exactly the gap discussed in the earlier Comparing RMSE Against MAE section. RMSE remains a genuinely useful, roughly intuitive number to communicate model quality with, just one that should be understood as somewhat skewed upward by any larger errors present, rather than as a perfectly literal average error size the way MAE more directly represents.
8. The Direct Link to Training

blocks.alt: Training loss of MSE gets reported as the RMSE metric

blocks.text: Because RMSE is computed by applying a monotonic transformation, the square root, directly to MSE, and because a monotonic transformation preserves the relative ordering of values, minimizing MSE during model training is mathematically equivalent to minimizing RMSE: whichever set of model parameters achieves the lowest possible MSE on a given dataset also, automatically and necessarily, achieves the lowest possible RMSE on that exact same dataset.

This is precisely why so many regression algorithms across the Regression module actually train by minimizing MSE directly, the mathematically smoother, easier-to-optimize quantity covered in the previous topic, while final results are very often reported to humans as RMSE instead, the more directly interpretable, original-unit quantity covered in this one. The two metrics are, in this specific mathematical sense, simply two different views onto the exact same underlying optimization target.
9. When RMSE Is the Natural Default

blocks.alt: RMSE is the most commonly reported regression metric

blocks.text: RMSE is the natural default choice whenever a single metric needs to capture both a genuine sensitivity to large, potentially important errors and directly interpretable, communicable units simultaneously, which describes the majority of general-purpose regression evaluation reporting encountered in practice. It is also the natural choice whenever comparing results against published benchmarks, academic papers, or competition leaderboards, since RMSE is very often the specific metric those external comparisons already report.

It is additionally worth computing RMSE alongside MAE specifically to directly compare typical error size against error-with-outlier-sensitivity, exactly the diagnostic technique covered earlier in this topic, revealing whether a small number of larger errors are meaningfully inflating the overall picture of model quality beyond what the more everyday, typical error size would otherwise suggest.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below computes RMSE alongside MAE and MSE for the same house price predictions, directly comparing all three metrics and their relationship to each other.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

actual = np.array([250, 310, 180, 420, 275, 390, 205, 800])  # includes one unusual luxury property
predicted = np.array([245, 305, 190, 400, 280, 375, 210, 650])

mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted)
mse = mean_squared_error(actual, predicted)
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)

print("MAE: ", round(mae, 2), "thousand dollars")
print("MSE: ", round(mse, 2), "(thousand dollars) squared")
print("RMSE:", round(rmse, 2), "thousand dollars")

print(f"\nRMSE is {rmse / mae:.2f}x larger than MAE")
print("This gap reflects the luxury property's outsized influence on the squared-error calculation")

# Confirm minimizing MSE and minimizing RMSE always agree on which model is better
predicted_alt = np.array([248, 300, 185, 410, 278, 380, 208, 700])  # a slightly different model
mse_alt = mean_squared_error(actual, predicted_alt)
rmse_alt = np.sqrt(mse_alt)
print(f"\nAlternate model: MSE={mse_alt:.2f}, RMSE={rmse_alt:.2f}")
print("Lower MSE model also has lower RMSE:", (mse_alt < mse) == (rmse_alt < rmse))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The final check confirms the monotonic relationship covered in this topic directly: whichever model achieves the lower MSE also always achieves the lower RMSE, since the square root transformation never changes the relative ranking between two MSE values.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: RMSE takes the square root of MSE, restoring interpretable original units while preserving MSE's outlier sensitivity.
It combines MSE's sensitivity to large errors with MAE's directly interpretable, original-unit results.
RMSE is always greater than or equal to MAE for the same predictions; a large gap signals a few dominant large errors.
This combination of properties has made RMSE the most commonly reported regression evaluation metric in practice.
The square root does not undo MSE's outlier sensitivity, it only fixes the unit-squaring problem, by design.
RMSE is roughly interpretable as a typical error size, though skewed upward relative to MAE whenever large errors exist.
Because the square root is monotonic, minimizing MSE during training is mathematically equivalent to minimizing RMSE.
This is why models often train on MSE directly while results are reported as RMSE for interpretability.
Next up: RMSLE, which applies a logarithmic transformation before computing RMSE, suited to skewed targets spanning orders of magnitude.
